panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 4 panels (A, B, C, D). A: Panel A shows the upper part of the lungs, which is consistent with the overall description of fibrotic idiopathic nonspecific interstitial pneumonia and associated ground-glass opacities. B: Panel B shows the middle part of the lungs, consistent with the described CT pattern of fibrotic idiopathic nonspecific interstitial pneumonia. C: Panel C shows the lower part of the lungs, which is a critical area for demonstrating features like traction bronchiectasis and bronchiolectasis associated with fibrotic idiopathic nonspecific interstitial pneumonia. D: Panel D provides a sagittal view (MIP) of the lung pathology, showing the distribution of fibrotic changes consistent with idiopathic nonspecific interstitial pneumonia.

panels.figure_caption: Computed tomography of a male patient with anti-Ku antibodies, demonstrating a pattern of fibrotic nonspecific interstitial pneumonia, apicobasal distribution of ground-glass opacities and reticulation with subpleural sparing, bronchiectasis, and bronchiolectasis, associated with paraseptal emphysema. (A) Upper part of the lungs, axial view. (B) Middle part of the lungs, axial view. (C) Lower part of the lungs, axial view. (D) Sagittal view, with a minimal intensity projection of 5 mm.
in_text_mentions: The most frequent radiological pattern was nonspecific interstitial pneumonia (NSIP), identified in 10 cases (53%); two additional cases had a pattern of NSIP/organizing pneumonia overlap (Figure 3 and Figure 4). No significant difference was observed in the distribution of patterns according to the underlying diagnosis of autoimmune disease.

plate_findings.evidence: CT scan demonstrating NSIP pattern contrast to UIP characteristics

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 4 panels (A, B, C, D). A: The panel is a CT scan clearly showing bilateral patchy ground-glass opacities and linear opacities characteristic of idiopathic NSIP, as described in the caption. B: The panel is a CT scan demonstrating chest pathology consistent with NSIP, specifically ground-glass opacities in the lower lobes. C: The panel is a CT scan showing basal ground-glass opacities and consolidation, which aligns with the clinical description of idiopathic NSIP. D: The panel is a CT scan displaying the characteristic basal ground-glass opacities and linear opacities associated with idiopathic NSIP.
panels.attribution_text: Tafti et al. Comparison of clinicoradiologic manifestation of nonspecific interstitial pneumonia and usual interstitial pneumonia/idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis: a report from NRITLD.. Annals of thoracic medicine 2008. doi:10.4103/1817-1737.43081. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 2.
panels.figure_caption: CT scans in nonspecific interstitial pneumonia
in_text_mentions: In this study, although the mode of onset of UIP was seen to be different from that of NSIP, the differences between the symptoms or signs were not readily apparent. The most significant finding in HRCT was the presence of bilateral patchy areas of ground-glass opacity, frequently accompanied by areas of consolidation and irregular linear opacities in the lower zone distribution. NSIP could be differentiated from UIP by the lack of subpleural honeycombing in the former, the most characteristic difference between the two diseases [Figures 1and 2].

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 4 panels (A, B, C, D). A: CT image (axial view) demonstrating classic findings of fibrotic idiopathic NSIP, including reticulation, ground-glass opacities, and traction bronchiectasis/bronchiolectasis in a male patient with anti-Ku antibodies. B: CT image (sagittal view) demonstrating the typical apicobasal distribution of parenchymal disease associated with fibrotic NSIP. C: CT image (coronal view) demonstrating the extensive interstitial reticulation characteristic of NSIP across both lungs. D: CT image (sagittal view, MIP) confirming diffuse parenchymal involvement and demonstrating the distribution of ground-glass opacities consistent with NSIP.

panels.rationale: This is an HRCT image of an adolescent, explicitly identified in the article title and text as showing NSIP. The image shows extensive bilateral consolidations, which is a known severe manifestation of the target disease. The findings support the diagnosis of idioptisch_nonspecific_interstitial_pneumonia.
panels.attribution_text: Cerro Chiang et al. Severe Nonspecific Interstitial Pneumonia (NSIP) in an Adolescent.. Case reports in pulmonology 2022. doi:10.1155/2022/7757776. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 2.
panels.figure_caption: Axial high-resolution CT demonstrates extensive bilateral peribronchovascular consolidations with air bronchograms, as well as scattered small nodular opacities.
in_text_mentions: Chest radiography on admission showed bilateral basilar interstitial infiltrates and confluent consolidations (Figure 1). An initial CT of the chest showed diffuse bilateral consolidations with central predominance and apical sparring. These consolidations did not spare the pleural space, and there were no traction bronchiectasis, fibrotic changes, or pleural effusions (Figures 2 and 3). The differential diagnosis included organizing pneumonia, viral pneumonia with acute lung injury, or connective tissue disease ILD.
